blocks.text: Welcome to Your AI Video Studio

You've probably seen AI-generated videos — some cinematic, some educational, some surprisingly realistic. What you might not know is that the tool behind many of them just got a major upgrade. In this course, you'll learn to create, edit, and direct videos with Gemini Omni, Google's most intelligent video model yet.
What Is Gemini Omni?
For a while, Google's video tool was called Veo — a specialized model focused purely on generating video from text. Gemini Omni replaces it with something much broader.

Omni is a unified model that works with any kind of input — text, images, existing video, even hand-drawn sketches — and can generate or edit video from all of them. It's is available through Gemini — Google's AI assistant — for all Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers globally. Turn it on by tapping "+" → "Create Videos."
What Makes Omni Intelligent?
Most video generators guess at what things should look like. Omni is built on Gemini's world knowledge — it actually understands what it's creating.

The Director's Script
You've seen how simple prompts transform into videos. Now let's look at how to actually build them — and what really makes a prompt work in Omni.
The Common Mistake

When most people first try Omni, they type something simple like "A cat in the garden." And Omni creates an aimless video. A cat appears, but there's no control over the result. The cat might sit, stand, or walk randomly. The camera angle is unpredictable. The lighting could go anywhere.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! A bare description gives Omni nothing to work with. It needs to know what's happening, where, and how you want it filmed.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The issue is a lack of direction, not the subject or length. Without action, setting, and camera guidance, Omni has to guess — and the results feel random.

options.label: The prompt lacks direction — no action, setting, or camera guidance
Simple description prompts are too short for Omni to process
Omni requires at least three sentences to work properly
Omni doesn't understand animal subjects well

blocks.question: Why do you think such simple prompts produce unfocused results?

blocks.text: So, the problem here is that "a cat in the garden" isn't a direction, it's just a description. Think about it: if you hired a film crew and said, "Film a cat in the garden," they'd ask a dozen questions:

• What's the cat doing?
  • Where exactly?
  • What's the lighting?
  • How should we frame the shot?
Omni needs the same information.
The Director's Blueprint

Great video prompts tend to cover a set of core elements — your blueprint that gives Omni what it needs to create a focused, intentional video: Camera Shot + Subject + Action + Setting + Lighting This isn't a rigid formula with a mandatory order. Omni is flexible — you can arrange these naturally, the way you'd describe a scene to someone.
What matters is completeness, not sequence. A prompt that covers all five elements gives Omni enough to work with. A prompt that skips half of them leaves too much to chance.

blocks.question: You want to show the full scope of a mountain landscape

blocks.text:
Camera shots tell Omni how to frame your subject. Here are some common options:
  • Wide shot: Full setting — ideal for establishing location
  • Medium shot: Waist-up view — good for action and dialogue
  • Close-up: Tight on a face or object — great for emotion or detail
  • Extreme close-up: Very tight (eyes, hands) — for dramatic emphasis
Choose based on what you want the viewer to focus on.
blocks.title: 💡 First Tip: Camera Shots

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! "Sitting" is technically an action, but there's no motion to animate. Something like "an old man flipping through a photo album, smiling at memories" gives Omni much more to work with.

feedbackIncorrect.text: While "sitting" is an action, it's essentially static. Omni needs movement to create an engaging video. Try adding specific, visible actions.

blocks.instruction: Evaluate this subject and action combination.

options.label: Strong, it has a subject and an action
Weak, the action is too static

blocks.question: "An old man sitting"

blocks.text:
The subject is who or what your video features. But without action, there's nothing to animate. Static actions like "sitting" or "standing" give Omni little to work with. Dynamic actions create movement:
  • Weak: "A chef standing in a kitchen"
  • Strong: "A chef tossing vegetables in a sizzling pan"
Always ask: What is my subject doing?
blocks.title: 💡 Second Tip: Subject and Action

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Golden hour light creates warmth and romance — perfect for this scene. A harsh overhead light would make the scene flat and unflattering.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Golden hour light is the better choice here. It creates a warm, romantic glow. Harsh overhead lighting works well for different moods, such as interrogation scenes or midday realism.

blocks.instruction: Now, decide which lighting works best.

options.label: Golden hour light
Harsh overhead light

blocks.question: You want to create a warm, romantic atmosphere for a couple walking on a beach

blocks.text:
Lighting tells the viewer how to feel. For example:
  • Golden hour: warm, romantic, nostalgic
  • Soft window light: natural, cozy, intimate
  • Cinematic lighting: dramatic shadows, film-like contrast
  • Neon lights: urban, vibrant, energetic
  • Harsh overhead: clinical, tense, exposed
Never leave lighting out; it's your mood-setter.

blocks.text: The Director's Script
You've seen how simple prompts transform into videos. Now let's look at how to actually build them — and what really makes a prompt work in Omni.
The Common Mistake

When most people first try Omni, they type something simple like "A cat in the garden." And Omni creates an aimless video. A cat appears, but there's no control over the result. The cat might sit, stand, or walk randomly. The camera angle is unpredictable. The lighting could go anywhere.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! A bare description gives Omni nothing to work with. It needs to know what's happening, where, and how you want it filmed.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The issue is a lack of direction, not the subject or length. Without action, setting, and camera guidance, Omni has to guess — and the results feel random.

Simple description prompts are too short for Omni to process
Omni requires at least three sentences to work properly

blocks.question: Why do you think such simple prompts produce unfocused results?

blocks.text: So, the problem here is that "a cat in the garden" isn't a direction, it's just a description. Think about it: if you hired a film crew and said, "Film a cat in the garden," they'd ask a dozen questions:

• What's the cat doing?
  • Where exactly?
  • What's the lighting?
  • How should we frame the shot?
Omni needs the same information.
The Director's Blueprint

Great video prompts tend to cover a set of core elements — your blueprint that gives Omni what it needs to create a focused, intentional video: Camera Shot + Subject + Action + Setting + Lighting This isn't a rigid formula with a mandatory order. Omni is flexible — you can arrange these naturally, the way you'd describe a scene to someone.
What matters is completeness, not sequence. A prompt that covers all five elements gives Omni enough to work with. A prompt that skips half of them leaves too much to chance.

Great job on learning the Director's Blueprint! Now, let's add the element that separates amateur clips from cinematic footage: camera movement.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to make your camera move with purpose.
Why Camera Movement Matters

Watch any movie or TV show closely. The camera is almost never completely still. It pans across landscapes, pushes toward a character's face during an emotional moment, and follows a hero running through the streets. This constant motion is intentional. It makes the video feel alive.

blocks.text: Three Essential Camera Movements
You don't need film-school vocabulary to direct Omni's camera. Three core movements will cover most of what you need:

• Pan — the camera rotates side to side or up and down.
  • Dolly — the camera physically moves toward or away from the subject.
  • Tracking shot — the camera follows a moving subject.
Let's explore each one.
Movement 1: Pan
A pan is when the camera rotates on a fixed point, like turning your head to look from left to right. Pans are perfect for:

• Revealing a wide landscape or location
  • Following the action that moves horizontally
  • Showing the scope of a scene
Common prompt phrases: "pan left," "pan right," "slow pan across."

blocks.text: Notice how the pan reveals the landscape gradually? Instead of showing everything at once, the movement creates a sense of discovery. That's how it works — it lets viewers explore the scene.
Movement 2: Dolly
A dolly shot is when the camera physically moves toward or away from the subject, like walking closer to someone or stepping back.

• Dolly-in: moving toward the subject (creates intimacy, tension, or focus)
  • Dolly-out: moving away from the subject (reveals context, creates distance)
Common prompt phrases: "dolly-in," "dolly-out," "slow push toward," "camera pulls back."

blocks.text: The dolly-in transforms a simple scene into an emotional moment. You can see that as the camera moves closer, we feel drawn into the woman's experience. This is why dolly shots are impactful — they control emotional distance.
Movement 3: Tracking Shot
A tracking shot is when the camera follows a moving subject — moving alongside them, behind them, or in front of them. Tracking shots are perfect for:

• Action sequences (chasing, running, walking)
  • Following a character through a space
  • Creating a sense of journey or momentum
Common prompt phrases: "tracking shot," "follow shot," "camera follows," "moving alongside."

blocks.text: The tracking shot keeps us with the cyclist, sharing the momentum and energy. This is what makes tracking shots immersive.
Choosing the Right Movement
Each camera movement serves a different purpose. Choosing the right one depends on what you want the viewer to feel or see.

You can now frame your shots and move your camera with intention. But there's an element that dramatically affects how your videos feel: lighting.

In the next lesson, you'll learn how to use light to set the mood, adding special atmosphere and emotion to ordinary scenes.
Setting the Mood With Light

In the previous lesson, you learned to move the camera with intention. 

But there is another element that creates atmosphere and shapes how every scene feels — lighting.

So, in this lesson, you'll learn how to use it to set the mood in each of your videos.
Think about your favorite movie scenes. Chances are, the lighting played a huge role in how they made you feel:

• A horror scene lit by flickering candlelight
  • A romance at golden sunset
  • A thriller with harsh shadows cutting across a face
Lighting tells viewers how to feel before a single word is spoken.

When you don't specify lighting in your prompts, Omni opts for neutral, flat scenes: evenly lit, no shadows or atmosphere. Think of the difference between a professional photograph and a quick phone snapshot. The subject might be the same, but the feeling is completely different.

Golden hour is the warm, soft light that occurs just after sunrise or before sunset. It produces balanced contrast and softer shadows on camera. Golden hour creates:

• Feeling of warmth and romance

  • A dreamy, flattering glow on faces and landscapes

Bringing Photos to Life

Welcome to Unit 2! You've learned the essentials of video generation, and now time to explore advanced techniques.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to transform still images into moving videos. Let's start!
From Still to Motion

Have you ever had an image you wanted to bring to life? It can be a family photo, an old memory, or a shot of a product you like. 

Omni can do exactly that: it doesn't just generate videos from scratch but also animates existing images, adds natural movement, and creates dynamic clips.
The process is simple:

• Upload your image
  • Add a prompt describing the motion you want
  • Let Omni animate it
  • Refine the result with follow-up prompts
Let's see how it works!
Starting Simple
Imagine you're creating a video greeting for your friend's birthday. You have a photo of yourself at a scenic mountain overlook and want to make it feel personal and warm.

blocks.exampleResponse: I'm generating your video. This could take a few minutes, so check back to see when your video is ready.
blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt to animate a photo into a birthday message.
blocks.template:
*Your image*
Turn this photo into a birthday greeting [subject action], [atmospheric element]

blocks.text: Look at the result!
You can use image-to-video to:

• Work with existing visual assets (product photos, portraits).
  • Personalize content (birthday messages, family memories).
  • Start with anything that's easier to photograph than to generate from scratch.
Also, it's often faster and more precise. When you already have the perfect composition, lighting, or subject in a photo, animating it gives you exactly what you want without multiple generations.
Directing the Motion

Now that you understand basic animation, let's add more control. You can guide not just what moves, but how it moves. This is where you combine what you learned about camera movement with image animation.

When animating landscapes, environments, or establishing shots, camera motion adds depth and energy. Remember: techniques like pan, dolly, and tracking also work with image-to-video. Let's try it with this image.

blocks.text: See how camera movement affects the result? A simple pet photo now feels like fun, shareable content — perfect for social media or just making people smile. This technique works beautifully for personal moments, creative projects, or lighthearted content.
Animating Memories

One of the most powerful uses of image-to-video is bringing old photos to life — family archives, historical images, or moments captured long ago.

This requires a slightly different approach: you want to add motion while preserving a photo's authenticity.
The key is subtle animation that respects the original image:

• A gentle head movement
  • A slight smile
  • Soft background motion
These will be just enough to bring photos to life.
Let's see how it works with this image!

Noticed the phrase "maintaining vintage photograph grain and texture"? That instruction tells Omni to preserve the photo's authentic character.

Without it, Omni might "modernize" the image — smoothing textures or changing contrast — which can erase what makes the photo meaningful.
Professional Applications
Image-to-video isn't limited to animating family. It's also effective for business and marketing:

• Product photos become dynamic social media content.
  • Headshots gain depth for testimonials.
  • Real estate photos turn into virtual tours.
  • Brand visuals feel more alive.

The principles stay the same: subtle motion, clear direction, appropriate atmosphere. The difference is your intent: you're creating marketing assets. For example, a product photo paired with "slow dolly-in, studio lighting, professional polish" can become compelling ad content in seconds.
Let's try a professional scenario. You need to create engaging ad content, and you have an image of these headphones.

Subtle motion, clear camera direction, and appropriate lighting produce great results.

Directing the Sound

So far, you've learned to work with visuals. But there's another dimension that affects your final result: sound.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to direct the audio in your videos — from ambient noise to spoken dialogue — instead of leaving those decisions to Omni.
Why Sound Matters

Until now, Omni has generated audio automatically for every video you created.

However, you can direct the audio yourself and control the mood, realism, and emotional impact.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Directing audio ensures it matches your intended atmosphere and mood. Without direction, Omni generates generic sound that might not fit your vision.

blocks.question: Why do you think directing audio is important instead of letting Omni decide?

blocks.text: Think about memorable movie scenes:

• Rain hitting a window
  • Distant thunder
  • A door slowly creaking open
These sounds create atmosphere and emotion just as much as visuals. And, you can design it in Omni!
How to Direct Audio

Directing sound in Omni works the same way as directing visuals: you describe what you want in the prompt.

The format is straightforward. Add phrases like:

• Ambient noise: [description]
  • SFX: [specific sound effect]
  • [Subject] says, "[phrase]"
Let's break down each type.
Sound Type 1: Ambient Noise

Ambient noise is the background sound that fills a space — the hum of an office, birds chirping in a forest, distant traffic on a city street. Ambient sound tells viewers where they are before they consciously process the visuals.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Without direction, Omni adds generic background noise or leaves the scene feeling empty. Specifying ambient noise gives your video depth and authenticity.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Omni will still generate audio, but it may feel generic, mismatched, or leave the scene feeling oddly empty. Directing ambient noise ensures it fits your specific vision.

Great! See how the ambient sound completes the scene? Without it, the café would feel unnaturally quiet. With it, the scene feels real.

This works for any environment — busy streets, quiet libraries, bustling markets, peaceful parks.
Sound Type 2: Sound Effects (SFX)
Sound effects are specific, noticeable sounds tied to actions — a door closing, footsteps on gravel, wind rustling leaves, a car engine starting. SFX adds realism to your video.
The key is being specific:

• "Wind blowing" is vague.
  • "SFX: strong wind rattling window panes" tells Omni exactly what you want to hear.
So, the prompt format for this type is: "SFX: [specific sound effect]."

The sound details place the viewer inside the moment. The footsteps, the breathing, the environment — all working together.

This is perfect for product demos, action sequences, or any scene where specific sounds matter.
Sound Type 3: Dialogue

Remember creating a birthday greeting in the previous lesson? It was actually done with the "Dialogue" technique. But instead of loosely suggesting speech, you can control the exact words that will be said.
Use this format: [Subject] says, "[phrase]" Keep it short. Remember that Omni generates a 10-second video at a time.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to direct the audio in your videos — from ambient noise to spoken dialogue — instead of leaving those decisions to Omni.
Why Sound Matters

Until now, Omni has generated audio automatically for every video you created.

However, you can direct the audio yourself and control the mood, realism, and emotional impact.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Directing audio ensures it matches your intended atmosphere and mood. Without direction, Omni generates generic sound that might not fit your vision.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Omni generates audio automatically, but without your direction, it may not match the mood or setting you have in mind. Specifying audio helps align sound with your vision.

options.label: Directed audio makes videos render faster
Omni doesn't generate audio without instructions
Audio direction is only necessary for dialogue scenes
It ensures the audio matches the specific mood and setting you want

blocks.question: Why do you think directing audio is important instead of letting Omni decide?

blocks.text: Think about memorable movie scenes:

• Rain hitting a window
  • Distant thunder
  • A door slowly creaking open
These sounds create atmosphere and emotion just as much as visuals. And, you can design it in Omni!
How to Direct Audio

Directing sound in Omni works the same way as directing visuals: you describe what you want in the prompt.

The format is straightforward. Add phrases like:

• Ambient noise: [description]
  • SFX: [specific sound effect]
  • [Subject] says, "[phrase]"
Let's break down each type.
Sound Type 1: Ambient Noise

Ambient noise is the background sound that fills a space — the hum of an office, birds chirping in a forest, distant traffic on a city street. Ambient sound tells viewers where they are before they consciously process the visuals.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Without direction, Omni adds generic background noise or leaves the scene feeling empty. Specifying ambient noise gives your video depth and authenticity.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Omni will still generate audio, but it may feel generic, mismatched, or leave the scene feeling oddly empty. Directing ambient noise ensures it fits your specific vision.

options.label: The video generates without audio
Omni automatically chooses the perfect ambient sound
Omni adds generic background noise that might not fit your scene
The video takes longer to generate

blocks.question: What happens when you don't specify ambient noise in your prompt?

blocks.text: To control ambient sound, use this prompt: "Ambient noise: [specific sound]."

blocks.exampleResponse: I'm generating your video. This could take a few minutes, so check back to see when your video is ready.
blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt to create a realistic café atmosphere.
blocks.template: Medium shot of a woman working on a laptop in a cozy café, warm afternoon light streaming through windows. Ambient noise: [object sound] and [people sound].

screens.title: Add Ambient Sound to a Café Scene

blocks.text:
Great! See how the ambient sound completes the scene? Without it, the café would feel unnaturally quiet. With it, the scene feels real.

This works for any environment — busy streets, quiet libraries, bustling markets, peaceful parks.
Sound Type 2: Sound Effects (SFX)
Sound effects are specific, noticeable sounds tied to actions — a door closing, footsteps on gravel, wind rustling leaves, a car engine starting. SFX adds realism to your video.
The key is being specific:

• "Wind blowing" is vague.
  • "SFX: strong wind rattling window panes" tells Omni exactly what you want to hear.
So, the prompt format for this type is: "SFX: [specific sound effect]."

blocks.exampleResponse: I'm generating your video. This could take a few minutes, so check back to see when your video is ready.
blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt to add realistic sound effects.
blocks.template: Tracking shot following a runner through a forest trail at dawn, golden morning light. SFX: [runner sounds] and [breathing sounds].

screens.title: Add Sound Effects to an Action Scene

blocks.text:
The sound details place the viewer inside the moment. The footsteps, the breathing, the environment — all working together.

This is perfect for product demos, action sequences, or any scene where specific sounds matter.
Sound Type 3: Dialogue

Remember creating a birthday greeting in the previous lesson? It was actually done with the "Dialogue" technique. But instead of loosely suggesting speech, you can control the exact words that will be said.
Use this format: [Subject] says, "[phrase]" Keep it short. Remember that Omni generates a 10-second video at a time.

blocks.exampleResponse: I'm generating your video. This could take a few minutes, so check back to see when your video is ready.
blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt to create a video with spoken dialogue.
blocks.template: Close-up of a coach standing on a soccer field at sunset, looking directly at the camera. [Subject] says, "[phrase]". Ambient noise: [background sound].

blocks.text: Here, we did one more thing — combined the dialogue with ambient noise.

This approach is the most effective because videos often combine multiple audio elements. For example: ambient noise for atmosphere, SFX for specific actions, and dialogue when appropriate. You can layer these in a single prompt, just like you layer visual elements.

blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt using ambient noise, SFX, and dialogue.

blocks.text:
See? Each sound plays a role. The dialogue communicates welcome, the door creak adds realism, and the rain sets the atmosphere.

This is how you create a complete experience — by directing every layer of the video.

• Ambient noise sets the environment and atmosphere: Be specific.
  • Sound effects (SFX) add realism to specific actions: Describe exactly what you want to hear.
  • Dialogue brings characters to life: Use the format "[Subject] says, '[line]'" and keep it under five seconds.
  • Layer audio elements for complete, immersive videos.

Keeping Subjects Consistent

Imagine you're creating a series of videos featuring the same person — a product demo host, a character in a story, or yourself in different scenarios.

With Omni, you can keep the subjects consistent so that they don't look different each time. Let's learn how!
The Consistency Problem

Without guidance, generating the same-looking person across separate sessions is surprisingly tricky — even with identical descriptions.

But within a single session, Omni keeps your character consistent automatically.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Consistency creates professional continuity. When viewers see the same person across videos, it builds recognition and makes your content feel intentional and polished.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Consistency isn't Omni's technical requirement, but it adds professionalism and recognition. When the same character appears across videos, viewers can follow along naturally, and your content feels cohesive and intentional.

options.label: It creates professional continuity and helps viewers recognize the same person
Omni requires consistency for proper audio generation, and it is important for animated content
Consistent characters generate faster than random ones

blocks.question: Why do you think maintaining visual consistency matters for a video series?

blocks.text:
You might describe "a woman in her 30s with brown hair wearing a red jacket," but each video shows someone slightly different — a different face, hair length, or jacket shade.

This breaks the continuity and makes your content feel disconnected.
The Solution

Omni solves this in two ways: through session continuity and reference images.

Stay in the same session and Omni anchors your character from the first generation — no extra steps needed. If you start a new session or notice drift, upload a reference photo to re-anchor.
The workflow looks like this:

1. Upload a clear photo of the person or product — or describe them in your first prompt.
  2. Generate your first video.
  3. Continue in the same session with follow-up prompts.
  4. If drift occurs or you start a new session, re-upload the reference image.

Using this approach feels similar to image-to-video, but the purpose is different.

You're not animating the photo. You're using it to re-anchor Omni to who or what should appear — especially useful across sessions or when consistency slips.

Let's take this image as a reference. 

We'll use it to create multiple videos featuring the same person in different scenarios.

blocks.prompt: Complete this prompt to generate a video with a specific person.

*Your reference image*
Medium shot of [subject] walking through [setting], [lighting]. The person [action].

blocks.prompt: Now, run this prompt in the same session.
blocks.template: [Camera shot] of this person [action] [location], [lighting]
tokens: typing on a laptop and thinking

blocks.text:
See? The same person appears in both videos.

Locations, actions, and lighting changed, but the character remained consistent. That's session continuity at work — and reference images as your safety net when it drifts.
What Makes a Good Reference
However, not all reference photos work equally well. To get the best results, your image should follow certain guidelines.

feedbackCorrect.text: Good reference images are clear, well-lit, show features directly, and avoid distractions. Think passport photo quality — simple and detailed.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Reference images need clarity and visibility above all. Avoid heavy shadows, sunglasses, blurry shots, or artistic angles that obscure features. Clear, direct, well-lit photos work best.

options.label: Neutral background that doesn't distract from the subject
Clear, well-lit photo with fully visible facial features
Direct angle showing the subject head-on or at a slight angle
Artistic photos with dramatic shadows and creative angles

blocks.question: What do you think makes a good reference image?

blocks.text:
The easier it is to see details, the more reliably Omni can reproduce them.

Always choose simple, clear, and well-lit over artistic.
Using References for Products

References aren't only for people. They work just as well for products.

Imagine you're creating a series of videos showcasing the same product in different settings: on a desk, in a bag, being used outdoors.
The process is the same:

• Upload a clear product photo as your reference.
  • Generate videos showing that exact product in various contexts.

Let's try it with this product example. 

We'll create multiple videos showcasing the same earbuds in different settings.

blocks.text:
See? The product stays consistent in both settings. 

This lets you show your product in different scenarios without needing constant shoots.

You've seen how references work for both people and products.

Now let's test your understanding of when and how to use them effectively.

feedbackIncorrect.text: References are essential when you need the same recognizable person or product across multiple videos. For one-off content showcasing variety, references aren't necessary.

Creating a five-video cooking series where the same chef demonstrates different recipes

From First to Last Frames

So far, you've learned to create individual videos with precision. But what happens when you want several clips feel like a smooth, flowing story?

In this lesson, you'll learn how to control exactly how your videos start and end, creating seamless transitions between scenes. Let's see how it's done!
The Transition Challenge
Often, you might have a clear vision of how you want your video to start and end, but the results from your prompts just don't click:

• One video might end mid-step without the desired final shot.
  • Another, vice versa, starts in a weird way.
This is where controlling the start and end frames can help.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Controlling frames lets you create smooth transitions between clips for a continuous story.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start and end frames aren't technical requirements; they're a storytelling tool. When you control how videos begin and end, you can connect them seamlessly into a cohesive narrative.

blocks.question: Why do you think controlling start and end frames matters for video storytelling?

blocks.text:
Professional videos feel smooth because transitions between scenes are natural.

The end of one shot flows seamlessly into the beginning of the next.

With Omni, you can design that flow using start and end frames.

Managing the Pace

By this point, you've learned how to create individual videos, keep your characters consistent across them, and create transitions. But what if you want to tell a story that lasts a little longer than what you have created so far?

In this lesson, you'll learn how to extend videos beyond Omni's default length to tell a complete story!
The 10-Second Limit

Omni generates videos up to 10 seconds long. This is ideal for capturing a single moment, but many stories need more time.

A short narrative, a product demonstration, or a tutorial might need 20, 30, or even 60 seconds to unfold effectively.
The solution isn't fighting the limit; it's working with it.

blocks.text: Planning Your Story

To make multi-scene videos work smoothly, you need a plan before you generate them. This is where Gemini can become your creative partner.

You can use it to:

• Describe your story idea
  • Ask for a storyboard
  • Receive a scene-by-scene breakdown of your video
You then generate each scene with Omni — refining conversationally with follow-up prompts until you're happy with it before moving to the next.

For example, you might ask:

"I want to create a 20-second video showing someone's morning routine: waking up, making coffee, and heading out the door. Break this into 3-4 scenes. Include scene descriptions, reference image prompts, video generation prompts, and timing suggestions for each scene."

By requesting all these elements upfront, Gemini gives you everything you need in one response.
So, when requesting a storyboard, ask Gemini to include:

• Scene descriptions
  • Reference image prompts for consistent visuals
  • Video generation prompts to use in Omni
  • Timing suggestions for each scene
This will give you a complete blueprint before you generate anything.

Combining Your Scenes
Once all scenes are generated, combine them using any video editor.
Popular video editing options:

• Mobile apps: CapCut, InShot, iMovie (iOS)
  • Desktop (free): DaVinci Resolve, CapCut desktop
  • Desktop (paid): Adobe Premiere, Final Cut Pro
  • Online tools: Canva Video Editor, Clipchamp
Choose whatever you're comfortable with — the process is simple in all of them.
The basic workflow is the same everywhere:

1. Import your generated scenes.
  2. Arrange them on the timeline.
  3. Ensure smooth transitions between clips.
  4. Export one final video.
That's it. Your 20-second story is ready!

One thing to keep in mind: Omni generates audio independently for each scene, so ambient sound and music won't automatically match across clips.

In your editor, add a single continuous music track or ambient layer across all scenes — this is the simplest way to create audio continuity in the final video.

By this point, you've learned how to create individual videos, keep your characters consistent across them, and create transitions. But what if you want to tell a story that lasts a little longer than what you have created so far?

In this lesson, you'll learn how to extend videos beyond Omni's default length to tell a complete story!
The 10-Second Limit

Omni generates videos up to 10 seconds long. This is ideal for capturing a single moment, but many stories need more time.

A short narrative, a product demonstration, or a tutorial might need 20, 30, or even 60 seconds to unfold effectively.
The solution isn't fighting the limit; it's working with it.

blocks.text: Planning Your Story

To make multi-scene videos work smoothly, you need a plan before you generate them. This is where Gemini can become your creative partner.

You can use it to:

• Describe your story idea
  • Ask for a storyboard
  • Receive a scene-by-scene breakdown of your video
You then generate each scene with Omni — refining conversationally with follow-up prompts until you're happy with it before moving to the next.

For example, you might ask:

"I want to create a 20-second video showing someone's morning routine: waking up, making coffee, and heading out the door. Break this into 3-4 scenes. Include scene descriptions, reference image prompts, video generation prompts, and timing suggestions for each scene."

By requesting all these elements upfront, Gemini gives you everything you need in one response.
So, when requesting a storyboard, ask Gemini to include:

• Scene descriptions
  • Reference image prompts for consistent visuals
  • Video generation prompts to use in Omni
  • Timing suggestions for each scene
This will give you a complete blueprint before you generate anything.

Using Omni Responsibly

You now have all the tools needed to create professional AI-generated videos. But like any powerful creative technology, AI video comes with responsibilities.

Before finishing this course, it's important to cover a few ethical and practical principles. These aren't complex rules — just clear guidelines that help you use Omni confidently and responsibly.
Why This Matters

AI video technology is still a new territory. So, a few simple practices will help you use it responsibly, protect yourself legally, and build trust with your audience.

Think of these as smart habits, not restrictions.
We'll cover three key areas:

• Transparency about AI-generated content
  • Respect for people's privacy and likeness
  • Avoiding misleading or deceptive content
Transparency: Letting People Know
The most important practice is simple: let your audience know when content is AI-generated. This doesn't mean adding disclaimers to everything. It means being clear when it matters.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Transparency matters most when people might mistake AI content for real footage, or when you're sharing publicly. Being upfront builds trust and credibility.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Disclosure prevents confusion and builds trust. When content is shared publicly or could be mistaken for real footage, it's best to let people know it's AI-generated.

options.label: Only when someone directly asks you
When posting publicly or when the video could be mistaken for real footage
For commercial content, not personal posts

blocks.question: When do you think you should disclose that a video is AI-generated?

blocks.text: Disclosure can be simple and natural:

• Captions: "Created with AI" or "AI-generated video"
  • Descriptions: "This video was created with Omni"
  • In-video text: A small note in the corner or end credits
The goal is to be transparent about your process, not to diminish your work.
Built-In Transparency

Omni actually handles part of the disclosure automatically. Every video it generates is invisibly marked with SynthID — a digital watermark developed by Google DeepMind that's embedded directly into the footage. You can't see or hear it, but it permanently identifies the video as AI-generated, even if someone edits, compresses, or reposts it.
Respecting Privacy and Consent
When you use reference images of real people, basic courtesy applies: make sure you have permission. This is especially important when creating content featuring someone's likeness.

feedbackCorrect.text: Permission matters in all these cases: when content is public, commercial, or could affect someone professionally.

feedbackIncorrect.text: All correct! The key principle is simple: get permission when content is public, commercial, or professional. Personal projects shared privately with the people involved typically don't require formal permission.

options.label: Making public content using a friend's image
Using someone's professional headshot for commercial purposes
Creating a promotional video featuring a colleague's photo

blocks.question: In which scenarios do you think you should get permission before using someone's image?

blocks.text: Some simple guidelines:

• Your own photos — safe to use
  • Family/friends for private projects — generally fine, but ask if unsure
  • Public or commercial use — always get permission
  • Strangers or public figures — avoid or seek legal advice
When in doubt, ask. It’s the simplest and safest option.
Avoiding Misleading Content

AI video can create incredibly realistic content. This power comes with responsibility: never create content that deceives or misleads. This means avoiding content that could be used for fraud, misinformation, or impersonation.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Creative content clearly labeled as fiction or parody is fine. Creating deceptive content that misrepresents what someone actually said or did is harmful and potentially illegal.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The line is clear: creative, clearly fictional content is ethical. Content designed to deceive people about what someone said or did crosses into misinformation and potential fraud.

options.label: Creating a video of a politician saying something they never said and sharing it as if it's real
Creating a fictional short film where a character resembles a public figure, clearly labeled as a parody

blocks.question: Which of these two scenarios do you think is ethical?

blocks.text: Avoid creating content that involves:

• Fake news or misinformation
  • Deceptive impersonation of real people
  • Fraudulent product endorsements
  • Manipulative or misleading narratives
Creative, clearly fictional content is fine, deception is not.
Copyright and Intellectual Property

Omni generates original content, but you should still be mindful of copyright when referencing existing brands, characters, or media. The basic principle: don't recreate protected content without permission.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Original content inspired by general ideas is fine. Recreating specific copyrighted characters, scenes, or using brand logos without permission can cause legal issues.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Copyright protects specific characters, logos, and creative works. Original content keeps you on safe ground.

options.label: Creating original characters inspired by general themes for your content
Recreating a scene from a popular movie exactly and posting it publicly
Using a well-known brand logo prominently in your commercial video
Creating a video featuring a famous animated character in your product ad

blocks.question: Which scenario best respects copyright?

blocks.text: So, for public or commercial content:

• Create original characters and visuals
  • Avoid recreating specific copyrighted characters or brands
  • Seek legal advice when referencing protected material
  • Be cautions even with personal, non-commercial parody
When unsure, originality is always the safer — and more valuable — choice.
Building Trust With Your Audience

These guidelines are ways to protect yourself and build credibility.

Being transparent, respectful, and honest makes your content more trustworthy and strengthens your credibility as a creator.
Responsible AI use benefits you directly:

• Builds audience trust: People appreciate honesty.
  • Protects you legally: Following guidelines prevents issues.
  • Enhances your reputation: Responsible creators stand out.
  • Future-proofs your work: Good practices scale with your growth.
Think of ethics as a competitive advantage, not a burden.
Now that you're familiar with the key ethical considerations, let's wrap up with a quick checklist you can return to anytime you're creating AI-generated content.

When sharing AI-generated videos, always ask yourself:
  • Have I disclosed that this is AI-generated when posting publicly?
  • Do I have permission to use any real people's images in this content?
  • Is this content honest and not intended to deceive or mislead?
  • Am I avoiding recreating copyrighted characters or brands?
  • Would I feel comfortable explaining to my audience how this was made?
If the answer is "yes" to all, you're using Omni responsibly.

blocks.question: In which scenarios do you think you should get permission before using someone's image?

blocks.text: Some simple guidelines:

• Your own photos — safe to use
  • Family/friends for private projects — generally fine, but ask if unsure
  • Public or commercial use — always get permission
  • Strangers or public figures — avoid or seek legal advice
When in doubt, ask. It’s the simplest and safest option.
Avoiding Misleading Content

AI video can create incredibly realistic content. This power comes with responsibility: never create content that deceives or misleads. This means avoiding content that could be used for fraud, misinformation, or impersonation.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Creative content clearly labeled as fiction or parody is fine. Creating deceptive content that misrepresents what someone actually said or did is harmful and potentially illegal.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The line is clear: creative, clearly fictional content is ethical. Content designed to deceive people about what someone said or did crosses into misinformation and potential fraud.

options.label: Creating a video of a politician saying something they never said and sharing it as if it's real
Creating a fictional short film where a character resembles a public figure, clearly labeled as a parody

blocks.question: Which of these two scenarios do you think is ethical?

blocks.text: Avoid creating content that involves:

• Fake news or misinformation
  • Deceptive impersonation of real people
  • Fraudulent product endorsements
  • Manipulative or misleading narratives
Creative, clearly fictional content is fine, deception is not.
Copyright and Intellectual Property

Omni generates original content, but you should still be mindful of copyright when referencing existing brands, characters, or media. The basic principle: don't recreate protected content without permission.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Original content inspired by general ideas is fine. Recreating specific copyrighted characters, scenes, or using brand logos without permission can cause legal issues.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Copyright protects specific characters, logos, and creative works. Original content keeps you on safe ground.

Using a well-known brand logo prominently in your commercial video

blocks.question: Which scenario best respects copyright?

blocks.text: So, for public or commercial content:

• Create original characters and visuals
  • Avoid recreating specific copyrighted characters or brands
  • Seek legal advice when referencing protected material
  • Be cautions even with personal, non-commercial parody
When unsure, originality is always the safer — and more valuable — choice.
Building Trust With Your Audience

These guidelines are ways to protect yourself and build credibility.

Being transparent, respectful, and honest makes your content more trustworthy and strengthens your credibility as a creator.
Responsible AI use benefits you directly:

• Builds audience trust: People appreciate honesty.
  • Protects you legally: Following guidelines prevents issues.
  • Enhances your reputation: Responsible creators stand out.
  • Future-proofs your work: Good practices scale with your growth.
Think of ethics as a competitive advantage, not a burden.
Now that you're familiar with the key ethical considerations, let's wrap up with a quick checklist you can return to anytime you're creating AI-generated content.

When sharing AI-generated videos, always ask yourself:
  • Have I disclosed that this is AI-generated when posting publicly?
  • Do I have permission to use any real people's images in this content?
  • Is this content honest and not intended to deceive or mislead?
  • Am I avoiding recreating copyrighted characters or brands?
  • Would I feel comfortable explaining to my audience how this was made?
If the answer is "yes" to all, you're using Omni responsibly.
